title: How a 1× mountain-bike drivetrain works
summary: Understand why MTB M1 uses one front chainring, a wide-range cassette and a rear derailleur instead of front shifting.

steps.title: There is only one front chainring.
steps.body: A 1× drivetrain removes front shifting and uses one chainring at the crank. All selectable gear changes happen across the rear cassette.
steps.keyFact: 1× means one chainring at the front, not one gear overall.

steps.title: A wide-range cassette supplies the spread.
steps.body: Because there is no second front chainring, the cassette spans substantially different sprocket sizes so the drivetrain can offer easier climbing gears and harder faster gears from the rear.
steps.keyFact: Gear range comes from the relationship between the single front chainring and the available rear sprockets.

steps.title: The rear derailleur handles every shift.
steps.body: The rear derailleur moves the chain across cassette sprockets and manages chain length as effective sprocket diameter changes.
steps.keyFact: On this 1× layout, there is no front derailleur to coordinate.

steps.title: Chain control matters on rough terrain.
steps.body: Rough terrain accelerates the bike and drivetrain vertically. Modern MTB drivetrains use component geometry and derailleur chain management to help keep the chain controlled while still allowing shifting.
steps.keyFact: Chain retention is a system property involving chainring, chain, derailleur and chainline—not one magic component.

steps.title: Find the component that provides rear gear choices.
steps.body: Identify the stack of rear sprockets that supplies the selectable ratios in a 1× drivetrain.
steps.keyFact: The cassette contains the rear sprockets.

challenge.prompt: Which component provides the selectable rear sprockets?
challenge.successText: Correct. The cassette is the stack of rear sprockets.
challenge.retryText: That component participates in shifting, but it is not the sprocket stack.
